What is SQLite: SQLite is a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration SQL database engine. It's the most widely deployed database in the world — embedded in browsers, phones, IoT devices. The entire database is a single file. No separate server process needed.

sqlite3 --version
# SQLite 3.45.1

-- Open/create database
sqlite3 mydb.db
-- .databases
-- .quit
Installing SQLite: SQLite comes pre-installed on macOS and most Linux distros. On Windows, download from sqlite.org. Or use a package manager: apt, brew, or compile from source. The sqlite3 CLI tool is all you need.

# Linux
sudo apt install sqlite3

# macOS
brew install sqlite3

# Verify
sqlite3 --version

# Python (bundled)
python3 -c "import sqlite3; print(sqlite3.sqlite_version)"
SQLite CLI Basics: The sqlite3 CLI is the main interface. Dot-commands start with . (not SQL). Key commands: .tables, .schema, .databases, .import, .output, .mode, .dump, .quit. SQL statements end with ;.

sqlite3 mydb.db

sqlite> .tables
sqlite> .schema users
sqlite> .mode column
sqlite> .headers on
sqlite> SELECT * FROM users;
sqlite> .quit
SQLite Data Types: SQLite uses dynamic typing: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB. Type affinity (flexible): INTEGER affinity for whole numbers, REAL for floats, TEXT for strings, BLOB for binary. BOOLEAN stored as INTEGER 0/1. No separate DATE type — use TEXT, INTEGER (Unix), or REAL (Julian).

CREATE TABLE sample (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  age INTEGER,
  salary REAL,
  photo BLOB,
  is_active INTEGER DEFAULT 1, -- boolean
  created TEXT DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

-- Check types with typeof()
SELECT typeof(42), typeof(3.14), typeof('hello'), typeof(x'deadbeef');
SQLite Limitations: No concurrent writes (single writer, shared lock). No user management/authentication. 64-bit ROWID limit (~9 quintillion rows). 140TB max DB size (pragma page_size * max_pages). Limited ALTER TABLE (DROP COLUMN was added in 3.35, but no MODIFY COLUMN).

Transactions: SQLite has full ACID transactions. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK. SAVEPOINT for nested transactions (savepoints). IMMEDIATE/EXCLUSIVE transaction types control locking. WAL mode allows concurrent reads during a write.
Views & Triggers: Views: saved queries acting as virtual tables. CREATE VIEW, DROP VIEW. Triggers: automatic SQL execution on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. BEFORE/AFTER and INSTEAD OF (for views). FOR EACH ROW (only option — no FOR EACH STATEMENT).

CREATE VIEW active_users AS
SELECT id, name, email FROM users WHERE status = 'active';

-- Trigger for updated_at
CREATE TRIGGER update_timestamp
AFTER UPDATE ON users
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE users SET updated_at = datetime('now') WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

-- Audit trigger
CREATE TRIGGER log_deletes
AFTER DELETE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO audit_log(table_name, action, record_id)
  VALUES ('orders', 'DELETE', OLD.id);
END;
Indexes & Performance: CREATE INDEX speeds up queries. Types: single-column, composite, UNIQUE, partial (WHERE clause), DESC. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows query execution. ANALYZE collects statistics for better query planning. Use WHERE clause indexes.
Full-Text Search (FTS5): SQLite's FTS5 extension provides full-text search. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE using fts5. MATCH for searching. Supports stemming, ranking (bm25), prefix queries, and content tables (external content).
JSON Support: SQLite has JSON functions: json_extract, json_set, json_remove, json_array, json_object, json_each (table function), json_type. The -> and ->> operators work like MySQL. Use json_valid to check JSON validity.
WAL Mode & Concurrency: WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) allows concurrent readers during a write. PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL. Better performance for many reads + occasional writes. Checkpoint moves WAL content to main DB. PRAGMA synchronous controls durability vs speed.
VACUUM & Maintenance: VACUUM rebuilds the database file, reclaiming space and defragmenting. AUTO_VACUUM is incremental but less effective. PRAGMA auto_vacuum = 1 enables incremental vacuum. PRAGMA integrity_check verifies database health.

CREATE TABLE: CREATE TABLE defines a table. Column constraints: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, CHECK. SQLite auto-creates INTEGER PRIMARY KEY as ROWID alias (auto-increment). WITHOUT ROWID tables use the PRIMARY KEY as the B-tree key.
ALTER TABLE: SQLite supports limited ALTER TABLE: RENAME TABLE, RENAME COLUMN (3.25+), ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN (3.35+). Cannot MODIFY, ALTER, or ADD CONSTRAINT after creation. Workaround: create new table, copy data, drop old, rename.
DROP & TRUNCATE: DROP TABLE removes the table entirely. SQLite has no TRUNCATE TABLE — use DELETE FROM without WHERE. For large tables, DROP and recreate with same schema, or use DELETE and VACUUM to reclaim space.
Constraints & Foreign Keys: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON enables FK enforcement (off by default!). Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY. ON DELETE/UPDATE: CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, RESTRICT, NO ACTION.

SELECT: SELECT retrieves rows. Support for WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING. SQLite's LIMIT/OFFSET syntax is standard. Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to check optimization.
INSERT: INSERT adds rows. Standard VALUES syntax. Multi-row INSERT supported (3.20+). INSERT OR REPLACE / INSERT OR ROLLBACK / INSERT OR ABORT / INSERT OR FAIL / INSERT OR IGNORE for conflict handling. last_insert_rowid() returns the auto-generated id.
UPDATE: UPDATE modifies existing rows. Always use WHERE. SQLite supports UPDATE FROM (joins in UPDATE) since 3.33. No LIMIT in UPDATE — use a subquery or WHERE with ROWID.
DELETE: DELETE removes rows. Always use WHERE. SQLite supports DELETE FROM JOIN USING (since 3.35) and RETURNING clause (3.35+) to return deleted rows.
WHERE & Filtering: Standard WHERE operators: =, !=, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, GLOB, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL. LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII. GLOB uses Unix wildcards (*, ?). Combine with AND, OR.
ORDER BY & LIMIT: ORDER BY sorts results. NULLs sort first by default (change with NULLS FIRST/LAST). LIMIT restricts row count. OFFSET for pagination. For efficient pagination, use WHERE on indexed column instead of OFFSET.

String Functions: SQLite has practical string functions: || for concatenation, LENGTH, UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTR, REPLACE, TRIM/LTRIM/RTRIM, INSTR (find substring), LIKE/GLOB, || for concatenation. No CONCAT() — use ||.
Date & Time Functions: SQLite has no date/time storage type. Use TEXT (ISO-8601), INTEGER (Unix timestamp), or REAL (Julian day). Functions: date(), time(), datetime(), strftime(), julianday(). strftime uses C-style format strings.
Conditional & Math Functions: IIF(condition, true_val, false_val) — ternary. CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END for multi-way. IFNULL(val, default) replaces NULL. COALESCE returns first non-null. Math: ABS, ROUND, RANDOM, TOTAL, AVG, COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX.

SQLite with Python: Python's sqlite3 module is part of the standard library. No external dependencies. Connection, cursor, execute, commit, close pattern. Use ? placeholders for parameterized queries (never f-strings!).

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect('mydb.db')
c = conn.cursor()

c.execute('''CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users
             (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT)''')

# Parameterized query (safe)
c.execute('INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (?, ?)',
          ('Alice', 'alice@example.com'))
conn.commit()

# Fetch
c.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?', ('Alice',))
print(c.fetchone())

conn.close()
SQLite with Node.js: Use better-sqlite3 (synchronous, fast) or sql.js (WASM, browser-compatible). better-sqlite3: prepare, run, get, all, iterate. No async — synchronous is fine for SQLite's speed.
SQLite with Go: Use mattn/go-sqlite3 (CGO) or modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go). Standard database/sql interface. Placeholder: ?. WAL mode for concurrency.

package main

import (
  "database/sql"
  _ "github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3"
)

func main() {
  db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite3", "mydb.db")
  defer db.Close()

  db.Exec("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")

  tx, _ := db.Begin()
  stmt, _ := tx.Prepare("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)")
  stmt.Exec("Alice")
  stmt.Exec("Bob")
  tx.Commit()

  rows, _ := db.Query("SELECT id, name FROM users")
  for rows.Next() {
    var id int
    var name string
    rows.Scan(&id, &name)
  }
}
SQLite in Browsers: sql.js compiles SQLite to WebAssembly for in-browser use. Also: OPFS (Origin Private File System) with SQLite WASM builds from sqlite.org. Great for offline-first apps, demos, and tools.
CLI Tips & Tricks: The sqlite3 CLI is powerful: .mode for output (column, csv, json, html), .headers on/off, .output file, .import for CSV loading, .dump for backup, .read for script execution, .timer for timing.

# Working with CSV
.mode csv
.headers on
.import data.csv mytable

# JSON output
.mode json
SELECT * FROM users;

# Export to file
.output output.txt
SELECT * FROM users;
.output stdout

# Backup
.output backup.sql
.dump
.output stdout

# Load and run script
.read setup.sql

# Timing
.timer on

Window Functions: Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them like GROUP BY. ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique number, RANK() allows ties with gaps, DENSE_RANK() allows ties without gaps. LEAD() accesses the next row's value, LAG() accesses the previous row's value. OVER() defines the window; PARTITION BY splits into groups, ORDER BY orders within each group. SQLite has supported window functions since version 3.25. A common mistake is forgetting ORDER BY inside OVER for functions that depend on order (like ROW_NUMBER).

SELECT
  id,
  name,
  amount,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS row_num,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rank,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM sales;

-- Per-group ranking
SELECT
  department,
  employee,
  salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM employees;

-- LEAD and LAG (compare with previous/next row)
SELECT
  date,
  amount,
  LAG(amount)  OVER (ORDER BY date) AS prev_day,
  LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS next_day,
  amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS day_change
FROM daily_sales;
CTEs & Recursive Queries: CTEs (Common Table Expressions) use WITH to define a named subquery that can be referenced multiple times. WITH RECURSIVE allows self-referencing CTEs for traversing hierarchical or graph data. The recursive CTE has two parts: the anchor (initial rows, no recursion) and the recursive member (references the CTE itself). Must use UNION ALL. SQLite limits recursion depth with PRAGMA recursive_triggers and an internal max depth of 1000 (configurable). Common mistake: forgetting the UNION ALL between anchor and recursive members.

-- Simple CTE
WITH sales_summary AS (
  SELECT department, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM sales GROUP BY department
)
SELECT * FROM sales_summary WHERE total > 10000;

-- Recursive CTE: generate numbers 1 to 10
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
  SELECT 1           -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 10  -- recursive
)
SELECT * FROM numbers;

-- Recursive CTE: directory tree
CREATE TABLE directories (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  parent_id INTEGER REFERENCES directories(id)
);

WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, parent_id, 0 AS depth
  FROM directories WHERE parent_id IS NULL  -- root
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d.id, d.name, d.parent_id, t.depth + 1
  FROM directories d
  JOIN tree t ON d.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT * FROM tree ORDER BY depth, name;

-- Recursive CTE: Fibonacci sequence
WITH RECURSIVE fibonacci(a, b, n) AS (
  SELECT 0, 1, 1  -- anchor: F1=0, F2=1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT b, a + b, n + 1
  FROM fibonacci WHERE n < 20
)
SELECT a AS fib_number FROM fibonacci;
Full-Text Search (FTS5): FTS5 is SQLite's full-text search extension. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE USING fts5 creates the search index. MATCH performs the search. Supports prefix queries (*), phrase queries ("in double quotes"), and NEAR proximity searches. The bm25() function ranks results. FTS5 can use an external content table (content=) to avoid duplicating data. Use snippet() to get highlighted excerpts. Common mistake: forgetting that FTS5 is an extension that may not be available in all builds (check with PRAGMA compile_options).
Triggers: Triggers in SQLite run automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. BEFORE and AFTER control timing. INSTEAD OF triggers are used on views (since views aren't directly updatable). FOR EACH ROW is the only option (no FOR EACH STATEMENT). OLD.column and NEW.column access row values. Use RAISE(ABORT, 'message') to cancel an operation. Common mistake: triggers that recursively fire (Table A trigger updates Table A, firing the trigger again) — SQLite stops at recursion depth limit.
Views & Indexes: Views encapsulate complex queries as virtual tables. Indexes speed up lookups at the cost of write speed. Partial indexes index only rows matching a WHERE condition — saves space and improves speed for filtered queries. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows whether indexes are being used. The WITH clause can be used inside views. Common mistake: assuming a view with ORDER BY guarantees order (it doesn't — wrap in SELECT ... FROM (view) ORDER BY). Always use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to verify index usage.

WAL Mode & Journaling: SQLite has two journaling modes: DELETE (default) and WAL (Write-Ahead Logging). DELETE mode: changes go to a rollback journal, readers and writers block each other. WAL mode: changes are appended to a separate WAL file, readers can read the old DB while a write is in progress — much better concurrency. Checkpoints merge the WAL into the main DB (automatic or manual). WAL is faster for most workloads. Trade-off: WAL requires more file descriptors and is slightly worse for very large transactions. PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL is safe with WAL and faster than FULL. Common mistake: not setting WAL mode in applications with concurrent reads.

-- Check current journal mode
PRAGMA journal_mode;

-- Enable WAL mode (once per database, persists)
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;

-- Manual checkpoint (force WAL flush to main DB)
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint;
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE);  -- checkpoint and truncate WAL

-- Performance pragmas for WAL mode
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;      -- safe with WAL, faster than FULL
PRAGMA cache_size = -64000;       -- 64MB page cache
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;       -- wait 5s before locking error

-- Other journal modes
PRAGMA journal_mode = DELETE;     -- default, rollback journal
PRAGMA journal_mode = MEMORY;     -- fast but not durable
PRAGMA journal_mode = OFF;        -- no journaling (risk of corruption)

-- WAL file management (.wal and .shm files appear alongside DB)
-- To safely move a DB in WAL mode, first run: PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE);
JSON Support: SQLite has robust JSON support since 3.9.0. json_extract() extracts values, json_set() updates values, json_remove() deletes keys. The -> and ->> operators (3.38+) provide shorthand: -> returns JSON, ->> returns SQL text/integer/real. json_each() expands a JSON array into rows (table function). json_group_array() aggregates values into a JSON array. json_group_object() aggregates into a JSON object. Common mistake: assuming JSON values in TEXT columns are validated — SQLite does not validate JSON on insert unless you use a CHECK(json_valid(data)) constraint.
